2026-10-11 — **Failing tests for a lapsed account's relay and for terminal
Claude's keys and modes.** From the first QA run. A relay link that
reauthenticates as Free keeps carrying the streams it piped while Pro, so a
host shows its peer away while calls still reach it. Terminal Claude
switches on xterm's modifyOtherKeys as well as the kitty protocol: raw
attach does not know the leader in that form, and leaving attach resets
the kitty flags but not modifyOtherKeys, so the client's Ctrl chords die
afterwards. A permission cycled with Shift+Tab while terminal Claude is idle
shows only on Claude's footer, which amux does not read. Where Claude offers
auto mode, its plan menu has no accept-edits entry and its first entry starts
auto mode, which amux's "accept edits" choice picks; the fake terminal
Claude now draws that menu when its script offers auto mode.

2026-10-11 — **Failing tests for stopping and resuming an agent with an open
ask.** From the first QA run. A graceful stop waits for the turn to end, and
an open ask is a turn that waits on the very person who stopped it, so the
agent never exits on its own: the daemon kills it at the deadline, the next
incarnation records the stop as an unexpected end, and until then every
input, the interrupt included, is refused. A daemon that adopted an agent
from an earlier run has no pid for it, so that deadline's kill does nothing
and the agent can neither be stopped nor resumed. A Codex resume that Codex
refuses ("already has an active writer", the old server still running)
leaves the agent starting forever, because the interpreter drops an error
answer to its own startup request.

2026-10-11 — **Failing tests for phone attachments and previews from the
first QA run.** The phone sends a prompt's attachments with no placeholder
in its text, and the agent process builds Claude's prompt only at
placeholders, so every file and photo sent from the phone to Claude is
dropped (Codex appends them and survives). An agent row's preview is the
bare placeholder character when the reply opens with an attachment, on both
clients, because the fleet view takes the raw first line. The phone's
file-edit card says "Wants to edit a file" for a file it creates.

2026-10-11 — **Failing terminal-client tests from the first QA run.** The
words after a row of attachment chips wrap at the room the chips left on
their line, every line after; a multi-line answer in a question's own field
is drawn on one line; a file-edit approval cuts its path from the right, so
the file's name is the part lost; a long command's approval pushes its
choices and key line off a short screen; a refused rename at 80 columns
loses its way out; a new agent's settings edge drops the model and
permission before it shortens a deep folder; and a draft is dropped when
its chat closes. One test states a choice not yet made: an agent's single
line breaks stay line breaks, where the terminal now reads them as markdown
soft breaks. A passing test pins the documented promise that a draft typed
before an ask waits behind it.

2026-10-11 — **Failing tests for a host that cannot restart after a crash and
a Claude parent that cannot tell who reported.** Triage of the first
adversarial QA run. A daemon dropped in process (a crash in the test net, or
the phone's embedded runtime) leaves its relay link's task running: the
crash path drops the link's stop handle without stopping it, and the task,
which holds the profile's QUIC endpoint, keeps redialling the relay and keeps
the LAN port bound, so the host never starts again on its port. A child's
finished report reaches a headless Claude parent as a bare user message,
though the envelope names the sender and the kind and a Codex parent is told
`[agent <name> finished its turn]`. Both tests fail until the bugs are fixed.

2026-10-11 — **The QA tooling's tests pass on every CI runner.** testnet's
`ctl` test drives the terminal client in tmux, which the macOS test runner
lacked, so the test job now installs it there as the journeys job does. The
dump printer named a bundle's other files with the platform's separator, so
on Windows `client/fleet/state.txt` printed as `client\fleet\state.txt`;
it now uses `/` everywhere.

2026-10-11 — **QA testers run in Claude Code's auto mode.** A tester's shell
was a growing allow list of utilities in `dontAsk` mode, refusing loops and
`$(...)`, and it still could not hold a tool's arguments to the tester's
folder (`sort -o`, `uniq IN OUT` wrote outside it). Auto mode judges each
command against the tester's instructions, so ordinary shell work runs and
nothing waits on a person. `testnet` stays allowed outright so the
classifier never holds up `ctl`, and `git`, the web and subagents stay
denied. In a trial auto mode let a tester write outside its folder and read
the repository when asked to; the folder and the prompt are the
confinement, as before. A tester given a refused compound command carried
on with the rest of its work.

2026-10-11 — **A QA run cannot start from a topology file, and stopping an
ended tester touches nothing.** A topology file could declare fake hosts or
scripted agents, getting round the real-only check on `ctl host add`; in a QA
run `ctl up` now refuses one. Stopping a tester that had already ended walked
the process tree of its old pid, which may since belong to anything else; it
now does nothing.

2026-10-11 — **Ctrl-C ends a phone tester, and each tester reports its own
duration.** `wt exec` starts a phone tester's command in a process group of
its own, so stopping the launcher's group left the tester's Claude running.
Stopping now ends the tester's whole process tree and reports anything that
survives. The summary gave every tester the wave's length; each now reports
how long it ran.

2026-10-11 — **QA testers use real agents only and keep going past a refused
command.** A tester stands in for a person, who only meets real agents: in a
QA run `ctl host add` starts real providers and `ctl` refuses fakes, the
prompt has testers see a finding twice with real agents and hold a turn open
with a slow command for timing, and the fake-script repro moves to triage,
built from the capture's facts and provider recordings. Two testers in run
20261011-160731 ended three minutes in after one compound command was
refused, reading Claude Code's "Permission to use Bash has been denied" as
their whole shell. Their shell now also allows `sleep`, `cut`, `sort`,
`uniq`, `tr`, `seq`, `date`, `echo`, `printf` and `ps`; the prompt says
what runs (chains and pipes of those), what is refused (loops, `$(...)`),
that a refusal covers one command, and that there is no time limit.
`ctl tui paste` takes `--file`, since `$(cat file)` is refused.

2026-10-11 — **Removing a host kills only that host's processes.** Removal killed
every process whose command line contained the host's folder as text, so
removing `desk` also killed `desk2`'s agents and the net's tmux server, with
every terminal pane in it. It now matches the folder as a whole path and
leaves the tmux server alone. A flap now holds its hosts' edges weakly, so a
host killed or removed mid-flap still drops its edge and leaves discovery.

2026-10-11 — **A removed process host is gone for good.** Removing one ignored a
failed `amux server stop` and never withdrew the net's discovery announcement
for it, so browsers kept seeing the removed host. Removal now withdraws the
announcement, and kills whatever of the host's still runs until nothing does
(refusing to forget it otherwise), saying so when the stop failed.

2026-10-11 — **A flap keeps its period while a request holds the net.** The door
holds the net for the whole of each request, and a wait on a real agent takes
minutes; the flap's task took the same lock to flip the link, so a two-second
cut could last that long. A flap now cuts the link and takes a handle that
flips it, in process or at the LAN's gates, without the net.

2026-10-11 — **`ctl down` kills only its own net's serve.** If `testnet serve`
had crashed and the system had given its pid to another process, `ctl down`
waited a minute on that process and then SIGKILLed it. It now waits on and
kills the pid only while its command line is this folder's `testnet serve`.

2026-10-11 — **The QA summary reads a phone tester's result and an unfilled severity
correctly.** A phone tester's transcript starts and ends with the lease's own
lines, so the summary said it had no result. An unfilled finding's severity is
the template comment listing every severity, which counted as data loss. Lines
that are not JSON are now skipped one by one, the ledger records an unfilled
severity as empty, and the summary counts only a severity the field starts
with, otherwise unlabelled.

2026-10-11 — **A tester makes large files with `ctl make-file`.**
The attachments tester could not make a large file: its shell may only read.
A permission for `dd` or `mkfile` into its folder cannot be confined, since a
rule matches only how a command starts: `of=<folder>/../x` and a second
`mkfile` path both wrote outside in a trial. `testnet ctl make-file NAME SIZE
[--fill zero|random|text]` makes the file instead, refusing any name that
leads out of the folder, up to 2g.

2026-10-11 — **A QA tester signs amux off for its persona, and uses real agents.**
In a one-wave run every tester stopped after about 19 minutes while saying it
had not met its stopping bar, and closed with a list of what it would try
next. The prompt now has the tester signing amux off as ready to ship for its
persona, and ground that person would reach but the tester has not tried is a
risk it chooses to ship. Before ending it lists what it has not covered; what
it can do is its next task, and it ends only when everything left is
something it cannot do, each with why. Its closing `ledger done` gives what it
covered, its verdict for the persona and what it could not do; never what it
would try next. A new last step has it use at least one real Claude and one
real Codex agent, which two of four pilot testers had left uncovered.

2026-10-11 — **`ctl tui clip` takes any file name and always puts the
clipboard back.** An image's path went into the AppleScript that copies it,
so a name with a quote failed and a crafted one could run a shell command
from a tester confined to read-only tools; the path is now an argument. The
clipboard's text is put back however the paste ends, and the docs say that
an image or file copied on the Mac is replaced. `just qa --testers 1` works
again: the default number of phone testers is two or every tester, whichever
is fewer.

2026-10-11 — **Two more QA personas, and testers can attach files.**
A Codex-first developer works mostly with Codex on `gpt-5.6-luna`: approvals,
plan mode, and Codex's own view compared with amux's chat. An attacher puts
images and files into chats from the phone and the terminal client, many at
once, across hosts and through a bad network, held to what ATTACHMENTS.md
promises. The pool is now nine personas. To make attaching reachable,
`ctl tui clip PANE FILE [--image]` copies a file (or a PNG as picture data)
and presses Ctrl+V in the pane, holding the Mac's shared clipboard under a
lock across sessions and putting its text back after. `ctl phone attach AGENT
FILE [--image]` hands the chat's draft what the system's photo or file picker
would, through the debug door's existing attach request, since nothing outside
those pickers drives them.

2026-10-11 — **`just qa` runs two waves of four, stops on new findings only,
measures each tester's own memory, and asks testers to keep going.**
The pilot's two testers stopped after about six minutes, and its one memory
figure, 19.5 GiB, was mostly other software on the Mac. A run now defaults to
four testers a wave, two with phones, and two waves. A tester recording a
symptom the ledger already holds marks it with
`ctl ledger finding NAME --duplicate-of TESTER/NAME`, naming the earlier
finding as `ledger read` now shows it; a duplicate keeps its evidence but does
not count as new, so a wave of only duplicates ends the run. Each wave reports
how far the machine's memory in use rose over its level when the wave began,
and each tester its peak physical footprint, split into its Claude session,
its net with its agents, and its leased simulator: footprints rather than
resident sizes, which count shared pages once per process and add up to
32 GiB for one simulator. The prompt's last step now sets the bar for
stopping: every hypothesis tested and written up, the list grown twice from
what the tester saw, both themes, both terminal widths and a large text size
looked at, and no thin ground left in the ledger.

2026-10-11 — **Every real agent in a test net starts small and asking, a
re-added host is a new machine, and ledger entries stay whole.**
Only agents the net spawned itself started on Haiku or `gpt-5.6-luna` with
Claude asking; a child made by amux's spawn tool, or an agent left at the
phone's "Host default", ran on a large model, and terminal Claude took the
operator's own default mode, which acts without asking. The host's provider
commands now fill these in whenever amux names none: the Claude command adds
the small model and `--permission-mode default`, and Codex's scratch config
names the small model. A host added under the name of a removed one reused
its directory, so its daemon served the removed host's profile and agents
again; each host now gets a directory nothing has used. A ledger entry is now
written in one write, so testers recording at the same moment cannot
interleave their lines.

2026-10-11 — **A host with the phone connected can be killed or removed at once.**
The pilot QA run found that `ctl host remove` on a host the phone had been
talking to failed after thirty seconds and left the host half-declared: the
net waited for the host's LAN port as it took a daemon down, and in process the
port stays held while the phone's connection to the dead listener lasts, up to
two minutes. The wait now happens only when a host starts again, where the
port matters, with patience past that timeout; killing, stopping and removing
return at once. The same run found the phone tester started in the tree's
root, because `wt exec` runs there; the launcher now changes back to the
tester's folder inside the lease.

2026-10-11 — **A QA tester's net does not pass on the tester's Claude session.**
A tester is itself a Claude Code session, and the variables naming that
session reached every real Claude agent its net started, through `ctl up`
and through the launcher. Both now leave them out.

2026-10-11 — **Adversarial QA runs by hand with `just qa`.**
`just qa [--testers N] [--phone M] [--persona P...] [--waves W]` builds every
binary once, checks the operator's Claude and Codex logins with one real agent
each, and starts waves of Sonnet testers in a run folder under
`~/.local/state/amux-qa/`. Each tester plays a persona on a test network of its
own through `testnet ctl`, confined to its folder and to `testnet` and
read-only tools, reads only a snapshot of the docs and the QA guides, and keeps
its evidence in captures and a shared ledger. A phone tester runs inside a
simulator lease for its whole life. The committed `qa/` folder holds the base
prompt, seven personas, attack moves with the screenshot checklist, the
finding and ledger formats, a triage guide from finding to test, and a guide
to talking to agents whose every phrasing was tried on Haiku and
`gpt-5.6-luna`. `docs/QA.md` describes it; TESTNET.md documents `testnet ctl`,
growing a net, real providers, process and supervised hosts, the release feed
and the new faults; TESTING.md places QA beside the lanes, never in CI.

2026-10-11 — **Real agents on a test net start small, ask, and carry nothing of the operator's.**
Trying real Claude and Codex agents through every way a person creates one
showed four gaps in the test net's real providers. A spawned agent ignored the
model it was given and ran on the provider's large default; it now gets the
model named, or Haiku or `gpt-5.6-luna`. Terminal Claude with no permission
named took the operator's own default mode, which ran commands without
asking; a real Claude the net spawns now starts with `default`. Codex read
the operator's skills from the home directory and the account's plugins and
connected apps; it now runs with a home of its own and a config switching
those off, so every agent carries only amux's tool server and built-in
skills. A Codex agent can be spawned in plan mode (`--mode plan`). The
host's chat record that `ctl chat` prints now says what each item decodes as
and which asks wait on a person, and `ctl phone choose` picks an item of an
open menu, which the phone's model chooser needs.

2026-10-11 — **VoiceOver can choose Claude or Codex on the phone's new agent screen.**
The two agent cards on the phone's new agent screen were containers of
their texts with a tap gesture, which is not an action VoiceOver can take:
double-tapping a card did nothing, so a VoiceOver user could not switch the
new agent to Codex, and neither could anything driving the app through its
accessibility, such as the debug door. Each card is now one element with the
button trait and an activation that chooses it; its label and value are
unchanged.

2026-10-11 — **A test net can be grown, broken and driven from the shell.**
`testnet ctl` drives a served net one command at a time from a folder, for a
person or an agent exploring by hand: `ctl up` starts an empty net there, and
hosts, links and relay accounts are added and removed while it runs. Hosts
can be real `amux` daemon processes (`--process`), started, stopped and
killed as a person's would be and reached over their profile sockets, or run
under `amux supervise` (`--supervised`) taking releases the net publishes on a
local feed signed with the test key, including a broken build that never
starts so the supervisor rolls back. A host or an agent can use the real
Claude or Codex in place of the fakes, through wrapper commands that record
the provider's traffic with the probes and keep the operator's own settings,
tool servers and plugins out. With the LAN gated (`serve --gated-lan`, which
`ctl` uses) every route between hosts, however they paired, and from the phone
runs through a gate the net holds, so any pair can be cut and any host's
network given loss, delay, jitter, reordering or a rate cap; `flap` cuts a
link on a period. `ctl tui` runs the real terminal client in tmux and turns
its screen into the client's own frame format and a PNG through `shot`;
`ctl phone` drives the debug app on a leased simulator through its door.
`ctl capture` copies everything about a problem at one moment (topology,
session log, a dump of every host, provider traffic, screens, logs) into a
finding folder, `ctl dump show` prints a captured dump, and `ctl ledger`
appends to a QA run's shared ledger. Every `ctl` command is logged to the
folder's `session.jsonl`. A process host with discovery is announced on the
net's discovery bus by the net itself, because its daemon cannot reach the
in-process bus; a link to a crashed process host comes back once the other
side's connection times out. New harness tests cover growth, the new gate
faults, a process host's pairing, cut and crash, and a supervised host's
update and rollback; a smoke test runs `ctl` end to end.

2026-10-11 — **The Codex probe's own socket is short wherever it records.**
The capture proxy in `codex-probe` had Codex's app server listen on a socket
inside the capture directory. A capture directory deep in a QA run's folders
makes that path longer than a Unix socket's path may be, so the app server
never listened and the agent stayed starting. The socket now goes in the
temporary directory; the recordings stay where they were asked for.

2026-10-11 — **The test release key lives in the release crate.**
The private half of the release key debug builds trust was copied into two
test files, and the test network now needs it too, to sign the releases it
publishes to its supervised hosts. It moves into the `release` crate behind
a `test-key` feature that only test code turns on, and both test files use
it from there.

2026-10-11 — **A dump bundle prints as text.**
A dump's row, store slice and journal are binary protobuf that a person or
an agent triaging a bug cannot read. `dump-show BUNDLE [--agent A]`, a new
binary in `replay-support`, prints the manifest and, per agent, its row, its
journal in the interpreter's emission-golden format, the facts replayed
through the same renderer (or a line saying they match), its store rows with
order and revision, and its facts lines and checkpoints exactly as written,
so a line the redactor replaced hides nothing after it. Every other file in
the bundle is printed or named. The golden renderer gained a step-level
entry point that the fixtures' goldens share, so no golden moved. The
committed bundle's journal and its facts replay differ only in the
catalogue hash of the first frame, which the bundle predates; its test
leaves that line out and says why.

2026-10-10 — **The phone's auto-review row baseline shows the worded verdict.**
The phone words a Codex reviewer's verdict from its status ("Auto-approved")
with the risk beside it, where it used to show the reviewer's free text. The
component catalogue's auto-review example changed with it, but its reference
images were not re-recorded, so the iOS gate's component snapshots failed on
main. Both images are re-recorded; nothing else in the catalogue moved.

2026-10-10 — **A daemon takes what a paired daemon stamped as given.**
Only amux daemons call each other's peer service, and each stamps a
message's sender and a create's parent from its own callers. Three checks
re-verified that stamping on the receiving side and could only ever catch a
call made by hand: the peer service refused a create naming another host's
agent as parent, the receiving daemon refused an envelope whose agent sender
was not the calling host's, and replication dropped inventory rows a peer
listed for another host. All three are gone, with the forged-create and
impostor-envelope assertions that held them, and the docs now describe the
sending daemon's stamping instead. A peer's inventory still carries only its
own host's entry and agents, and the peer service still answers `NOT_FOUND`
for an agent its host only replicates rather than passing the call on.

2026-10-10 — **A resumed agent's row ends with its own cause, and a live row's cause is not filtered on.**
When an incarnation ends without writing its final boundary (killed, or
crashed), the next incarnation writes it on start and leaves that step without
a cause, because the earlier incarnation's row already says how it ended and
the commit would otherwise put the earlier end on the new, live incarnation's
row, where a later kill would keep it. A node test now resumes a killed agent,
checks the repair step and the live row carry no cause, and kills it again to
see `KILLED`; it fails without that clearing. The TUI's fleet filter matches a
cause only on an exited row, as the protocol says clients read it, and the
agents tool's test now gives a live row a cause the tool must not report. The
deletion ledger also catches Codex's ask opening time coming back, and a
stray row in the agent process's exit table is back inside the table.

2026-10-10 — **An agent's tools socket no longer refuses a person's calls.**
The client service on an agent's tools socket refused renaming, stopping,
resuming and deleting agents, storing blobs, reading diffs, listing
repositories and writing debug reports. The agent's tool server never makes
those calls, so the refusal only caught calls made by hand, and an agent can
run the `amux` CLI against the person's socket anyway; the check is gone,
with the assertions that held it. The socket still makes the caller a
created agent's parent, stamps it as a message's sender, and sends its input
only to its own direct children.

2026-10-10 — **An agent's exit cause reaches its row when the daemon ingests it.**
The daemon held the cause from an agent's last journal step in memory until
it marked the agent exited, so a daemon that ingested that step and stopped
before marking left the next daemon nothing to read, and its sweep recorded
"ended while away". Commit now copies `incarnation_end` onto the row's
`exit_cause` and `exit_detail` in the same transaction as the step, the way
it copies a snapshot's phase. Marking an agent exited only flips the
lifecycle, keeping a cause already on the row and recording the daemon's own
only where the row has none; a resume still clears the cause for the new
incarnation. The in-memory holding is gone. The agents tool, which words a
cause for any row that has one, now says nothing for a row still live.

2026-10-10 — **An agent's exit cause travels in its journal, and each client words it.**
The agent told its daemon why an incarnation ended in a last control frame,
and waited a moment for a daemon to take it; an agent that ended while no
daemon was connected lost its cause, and the next daemon wrote "ended while
away" over a drain or an orphaned ask it could have named. The step that
writes an incarnation's final boundary now also carries `incarnation_end`
(the cause and its own words). The daemon reads the journal to its end before
it marks an agent exited, on a live exit and on the startup sweep alike, and
records that cause; its own causes remain only for a process it could not
start, a directory that is gone, a process it killed, and a journal that says
nothing (`ENDED_UNEXPECTEDLY`, or `ENDED_WHILE_AWAY` when found on return).
An agent that cannot write its directory cannot write this either, so its row
says it ended unexpectedly. The `exiting` frame, its message and the
agent's farewell wait are gone. The wire crate no longer words causes: the
fleet and chat views, the TUI's filter, `amux ls` and the agents tool each
word the enum themselves. A child's failed report to its parent carries the
cause as data (`Envelope.ended`, set only on a failed report), stored as
the delivery's `exit_cause` and `exit_detail`, and each kind's interpreter
words it for the parent's model.

2026-10-10 — **The daemon no longer checks which input an agent sends its child.**
On an agent's tools socket the daemon refused any input but an interrupt.
The tool server only ever sends the stop tool's interrupt, so the check
caught nothing but calls made by hand, and it is gone with its test. An agent
still sends input only to its own direct children.

2026-10-10 — **A create names its kind by the arm that carries the kind's settings.**
`CreateAgentRequest` carried a `Kind` beside the kind's settings as opaque
bytes, which the spawning host decoded by kind and refused when they did not
decode; a well-formed config of the other provider could not be told apart.
The request now has one `agent` oneof whose arm is the kind: `claude_pty` and
`claude_sdk` take `ClaudeCreateConfig`, `codex` takes `CodexCreateConfig`, so
settings and kind cannot disagree. A create with no arm is refused as invalid
and makes no agent. The decode-by-kind, its refusal, the forwarding helper
that existed to pass the bytes through, and their two tests are gone; every
client (the TUI, `amux create`, the app runtime, the spawn tool, testnet and
qualification) builds the arm directly, and `amux` no longer needs `prost`
outside its tests.

2026-10-10 — **Exit causes sit with the records, and the shared input pieces with the chat vocabulary.**
`ExitCause` moves to `records.proto` beside `Kind`, and the input pieces every
kind shares (`PromptInput`, `WithdrawQueued`, `SendQueuedNow`, `Interrupt`,
`Clear`, `SetPermission`, `SetMode`, `SetModel`, `SetEffort`) move back to
`chat.proto` beside the answer pieces. They had been held in `service.proto`
only because `chat.proto` imported it for `ExitCause`; with that gone,
`chat.proto`, `claude.proto` and `codex.proto` no longer import the service
file at all. Nothing on the wire changes.

2026-10-10 — **An ask's records no longer carry when it opened and closed.**
The times added to an ask's close, a call's permission decision, a plan's
decision and a Codex ask in the snapshot had no reader, so they are gone,
with the helper each interpreter stamped them through and the tests that
checked their order. A Codex ask keeps its opening time privately inside
the interpreter, as before, for the item it closes. The interpreter goldens
return to their earlier lines.

2026-10-10 — **A paired host reads no blob of an agent it does not own, and the docs match the protocol.**
A paired host asking this one for a blob was answered from this host's
copy even when the agent was another host's, so a host could read the
attachments and patches of a third host's agents through a host it was
paired with. Every peer call that names an agent (reads, input, the
rename, stop, resume and delete calls, blob writes and reads, and diffs)
now answers only for this host's own agents and says not found for the
rest, as the reads and input already did; a test proves each one refused
on a replica whose rows and blob this host holds. A profile rename or
delete that names a stale revision was refused but nothing proved it; a
front-door test now does, and shows the refused call changed nothing. When
pairing is already open, `amux pair` also says that a demo window, which
no command holds open, closes with `amux pair --cancel`. The deletion
ledger bans the inventory's old last-activity field by its proto and
phone spellings again, instead of exempting the store's whole directory
for a column that shares the name, and the directory exemptions are gone.
Docs and comments that drifted are corrected: a create's config is decoded
as its kind says and a well-formed config of the other kind is not
detected; an agent sender carries no kind; a refusal is `REFUSAL_EXITED`;
a lagging inventory stream says `Lagged` before it closes; a replica's
last activity is written when a snapshot is absorbed, and replica
retention orders by phase start because every replica row has one; only
`rewind_cursor` is a bare `UPDATE`, outside any commit; and headless
Claude's statuses are listed once, as hidden journal items.

2026-10-10 — **The protocol's files say who reads them.**
`amux.proto` held errors, link control, pairing, both services, the
inventory and the front door, while the agent's private contract held the
public input envelope, and the session records held every shared chat body.
The definitions now sit in ten files of the same package, each for one
audience: `error.proto` (the carrier and its code), `link.proto` (host-to-host
control), `pairing.proto`, `front_door.proto` (profiles and the
installation), `service.proto` (`ClientService`, `PeerService`, the
inventory, their requests, `Input` with the input pieces every kind shares,
and the verdict), `records.proto` (the envelope records, `Kind`, agent
messages, attachments, blobs and diffs), `chat.proto` (the bodies, snapshot
pieces, asks, answer pieces and catalogue the kinds share), `agent.proto`
(the spec and the ctl and pty frames), and `claude.proto` and `codex.proto`,
which now also hold each provider's usage messages. Every definition moved
verbatim; the wire identity of a message is its package and name, so nothing
on the wire changed, and the generated Rust differs only in order. The
imports run one way: the agent's contract reads the services, never the
reverse, so the public vocabulary is not owned by the private one. The
exit-cause enum sits beside the inventory row; `Kind` stays with the records,
which name it and which every other file reads. Two wire types the phone
never receives as such, presence and a diff file's change, no longer derive
the serialization the Swift mirror is built from. The phone's code caught up
with two earlier wire changes it had not been built against: a permission
scope has no label, and a diff from HEAD is the base's `head` arm.

2026-10-09 — **The profile store is one SQLite schema, and a store from before it is refused by name.**
The store's schema had grown as a base and six alterations, three of them
written this week to turn kinds and exit causes into wire integers and to
drop a column nothing read. They are now one migration, the schema the first
release ships, with every column commented in its SQL text. Column names
say what they hold: times end in `_ms`, the item's wire order is `position`,
a parent is `parent_host` and `parent_id`, a name is never null, and a push
notification's name, working-on and text are three columns instead of JSON.
The snapshot's revision is read from the snapshot itself rather than kept
twice. A store written before this schema records a different first
migration, so opening it fails with an error that names the file and says
it predates the release schema; the daemon does not start on it and the
file is left untouched, for the person to move aside. The history is now
checked before the schema stamp, so such a store no longer reads as one from
a newer build. From the first release on, migrations only add.

The store itself is now the SQLite type alone. The in-memory copy that only
the store's tests used, and the row-primitive traits that let both share one
body of logic, are gone, so SQL does the work the traits kept from it: a
commit writes each item as one upsert that keeps a held key's position, a
replica takes an item only over an older revision in one statement, a pool's
bytes are one sum, and a cursor rewind is one update. Every row write to
agents and items stays an insert that updates on conflict, which is what the
daemon's crash-injection tests hook. Writing an agent's row updates only the
columns its writer owns, which fixes a replica losing its last activity each
time its origin's inventory row was put. Looking up an agent by id, a
parent's children and agents by name are queries, where seven daemon paths
used to load every row to find one. The conformance and retention suites run
once, against a temporary database file.

2026-10-09 — **The record of an ask says when it opened and when it closed.**
Once an ask closed, nothing said how long a person took to answer it: an
ask's item keeps the time it was first written, a Codex ask's item was
closed with its opening time, and the store keeps only an item's last
revision. Every record that outlives an ask now carries both ends: an ask
item's close has `opened_at_ms` and `closed_at_ms`, a call's permission
decision `asked_at_ms` and `decided_at_ms`, and a plan `decided_at_ms`.
A Codex ask in the snapshot carries `opened_at_ms`, as a Claude ask already
did. Each interpreter stamps them from its own clock as it observes the
ask open and close, since no provider puts a time on either. A decision the
provider made without asking amux (an auto-approval, Codex's reviewer, a
denial Claude made itself) has neither time. Nothing reads the fields yet;
the interpreter goldens print them.

2026-10-09 — **The daemon's link code calls a runtime's life a runtime instance.**
The random id a host's runtime draws when it starts, which a link handshake
carries so a peer can tell a restarted process from the one it already has
a link to, was typed `Incarnation` inside the daemon, though the wire field
is `runtime_instance_id` and "incarnation" means an agent's process count
everywhere else. The type is now `RuntimeInstance`, and the fields, locals
and the two link-registry tests that named it follow. Nothing changes in
behaviour.

2026-10-09 — **A lagging inventory says so, and the docs say what the protocol now is.**
A reader that fell behind the inventory's ring was closed without a word,
which every reader took for an outage: the fleet showed "reconnecting" and
backed off, and a paired host following the inventory tore down every
source it held for that host's agents and marked their chats stale. The
inventory now sends `Lagged` before it closes, as a chat's stream already
did. The fleet subscribes again at once, never reads as reconnecting, and
drops what the fresh listing no longer names at its `CaughtUp`; a paired
host follows again under the same session, so its sources keep running
while the listing reconciles the rows. Only a stream that ends without
`Lagged` backs off. The chat vocabulary's placement rule now says what it
always meant: a client draws a fact in at most one place, while the journal
may hold records no client draws, as long as each is durable, keyed and of
use to the daemon or a later reader (a compaction summary, an interruption,
a tool server's startup, a turn's whole diff). The protocol docs stop
claiming fields are never renumbered before release, describe refusals by
their enum, re-tail at once after `Lagged` in the client checklist, name the
diff's `head` base, and say that a replica's current catalogue survives the
blob sweep.

2026-10-09 — **One route vocabulary, one usage-limit vocabulary, and wire names that say what they hold.**
How this machine reaches a host and how a pairing peer was reached are the
same four answers, so a host entry's route is now a `RouteKind`, like a
pending pairing's, and `HostVia` is gone; the phone mirrors `RouteKind`.
Claude's and Codex's usage windows had identical limit enums, now one
`Limit`, and the overview words a window from it in one place. Names that
misled are renamed: a host-and-id reference to an agent is an `AgentRef`
(it names a message's recipient as well as a parent); an item, append or
snapshot names its agent as `agent_id`, like every other message; the link
handshake's 16 random bytes are a `runtime_instance_id`, so `incarnation`
means only an agent's process count; a host's `account_signed_in` is its
cloud account, not a provider's sign-in; a background job names the
`item_key` of the call that started it; and a diff from HEAD is the `head`
base. An append extends text on any open item, as its comment now says.
Every timestamp is `_ms`, Unix milliseconds, stated once at the top of
records.proto. The phone's permission grant names where Claude keeps it as
its `destination`, as the wire does. The daemon's own live-route enum,
which also says offline, is `LiveRoute`, so it is not mistaken for the wire
one.

2026-10-09 — **The phone's bridge names a provider through the app runtime again.**
Asking a host's catalogue by provider made the bridge crate depend on the
wire crate directly, which the dependency policy refuses: the bridge is a C
surface over the embedded runtime and the app runtime, and takes its types
from them. The app runtime now names the provider its catalogue call takes,
and the bridge uses that; the wire crate is back to a test-only dependency
of the bridge.

2026-10-09 — **A thinking row's "thought for" counts from the item before Claude's request again.**
Headless Claude's request status became a hidden item in the previous
change, and a thinking row measured its duration from whatever item came
just before it, so every "thought for" in headless Claude shrank to the time
since the request went out. The time Claude spent before sending the
request, after the person's prompt or the last tool result, is part of how
long it thought as the person saw it, so the duration now passes over status
items and reads as it did before they existed.

2026-10-09 — **A host only a free account's relay reaches is away, headless Claude's compacting status reaches the activity line, and fields nothing read are gone.**
The phone has drawn an away banner and an away host group since the free
tier began, and the docs promised that a host the relay sees while the
account has no subscription reads as away, but no daemon ever said so: such a
host was listed online, though the relay refuses to carry anything to it. The
daemon now lists a trusted host as away while the relay is its only route and
this profile's account is on the free tier; a profile is one account, so its
own tier is the peer's. A direct or SSH link makes the host online again, and
so does the account going Pro. Headless Claude reports "compacting" while it
compacts, but the interpreter ignored the status, so the activity line's
"Compacting" never showed outside tests. A status Claude names is now a
hidden item, typed as compacting or requesting with Claude's own word kept,
and the activity line reads it until the compaction row lands; a thinking
row's "thought for" now counts from Claude's request, which the status marks.
Removed because nothing produced or read them: terminal Claude's task
notification item (terminal Claude folds a task's notice into its call), the
`UPDATING` and `RESTARTING` link-close reasons, the relay's startup-failed
state and the phone's "The relay cannot be reached" line, the journal offset
in an agent's hello, the reason on a neighbour-down message, the provider
version on an agent's spec, the hook and environment lists of its effective
configuration (the agent always installs its default hooks, and the spec's
provider environment is the one environment), and the agent binary's version
on the inventory row and its store column; an item's own producer version is
the record of what wrote it. An agent row's `working_on` is the text alone:
its timestamp was the newest snapshot's time, not when the text changed, and
zero on every replica.

2026-10-09 — **The front door's calls are plain: no operation ids, flat pairing requests, byte ids, and `amux pair --demo` back.**
Eleven front-door requests carried an `operation_id` that the CLI minted
fresh for every call and the daemon never read: the replay ledger it once
keyed was dropped with the daemon rebuild, and no client resends a call. The
ids are gone, and the guarantee with them: a front-door call whose reply is
lost, which on the local socket means the daemon went away, fails and the
person runs the command again. Rename and delete keep their revision checks,
so a re-run cannot undo a change made meanwhile, and a pairing window lives
only in the daemon's memory, so a start re-run after a restart opens a fresh
window with a new PIN and nothing stuck refuses it. The pairing requests
lost their profile envelopes (`StartPairingRequest`, `BeginPairRequest`,
`PendingPairRequest`, `TrustSshPeerRequest`, `GetPeerRequest` and
`UnpairRequest` each name their profile), and answers that wrapped one
message are that message: `PairingWindow`, `PendingPair`, `PairingStatus`,
a `PeerEntry`, or `Empty`. A pairing start names its method in a oneof (a
one-shot PIN, a one-shot QR secret, or a demo PIN the operator chose) and
its length in one `ttl_seconds`, five minutes when absent and one second to
ninety days for every method; demo pairing used to carry a second TTL of
its own. The profile watch sends `ProfileEvent`s without sequence numbers,
and `ProfileInfo` lost `available`, `InstallationInfo` its paths. Profile
and host ids travel as their sixteen bytes, on SSH pairing frames and SSH
targets too; the CLI and the `amux relay --profile` argument use the text
form. A pending pairing's route is a `RouteKind`. A confirm or abandon that
names no token is now refused as malformed, where a missing token used to
read as a wrong secret. `amux pair --demo --pin <digits> --for <duration>`,
dropped with the CLI rebuild while the daemon kept the demo window, is back:
it holds a chosen PIN open for an unattended demo, such as an app review,
and returns at once; `amux pair --cancel` closes it. The protocol notes said
ordinary windows always last five minutes; the length is the start's to name.

2026-10-09 — **An agent tells its daemon why it ended, and the row says so; exit causes and removal reasons are enums.**
The inventory row's exit cause was a sentence only the daemon wrote, from
what it had asked for and what it saw, so a provider crash and a drain after
the daemon was lost both read "exited", and the fleet never showed "while the
daemon was away" for an agent that drained or "orphaned while waiting for
you" though the docs promised both: the agent's own cause reached only its
final boundary in the journal, whose body the daemon does not read. The agent
now sends one last control frame, `Exiting { cause, detail }`, before it
closes its socket, and the daemon records it on the row. A short-lived
incarnation that ends before its loop took the daemon's connection takes it
first, so a child whose one turn was quick still says it finished. The daemon
records its own cause only where no frame can arrive: the process could not
be spawned, its directory is gone, it was found dead when a daemon started,
a stop it asked for when the process ended without a word, and "ended
unexpectedly" otherwise; it no longer infers that a child finished. The cause
is an `ExitCause` enum with the cause's own words beside it (`exit_detail` on
the row, `cause_detail` on the boundary), and the store keeps it as its wire
integer, so a cause from a newer host is kept and listed as it came. Clients
draw finished, ended (a stop, or a cause they do not know) and failed in the
cause's words followed by its own ("the provider exited: exit code 1"), and a
parent hears a failed child in the same words. `AgentRemoved.reason` is a
`RemovalReason` enum: deleted, retention, no longer listed by its host, or a
host no longer trusted.

2026-10-09 — **Kinds, providers, refusals, scope destinations and reviewer verdicts are enums; a host's capabilities say what it can do.**
A kind travelled as a string (`"claude_sdk"`) on items, snapshots, specs and
agent senders, and a replica of an agent of a kind this daemon had no name
for was listed as unspecified; every kind is now the `Kind` enum, the store
keeps it as its wire integer, and an unknown kind is listed and replicated
with its number. `AgentSender` lost its kind. `GetCatalogueRequest` and
`ProviderOnHost` name a `Provider` enum; the `amux catalogue` helper and its
files keep the provider's lower-case word, derived from the enum's name. A
rejected input is `Rejected { Refusal refusal; optional string detail }`
instead of a free word, so terminal Claude's send-now refusal is
`REFUSAL_UNSUPPORTED` with its sentence as the detail, and clients show the
detail when there is one and their own words otherwise. A Claude permission
scope is `ScopeChoice { index, ClaudeGrant grant }`, and the grant names its
destination as a `ScopeDestination` with Claude's own word beside it, in
place of `saved_to` and the scope's label. Codex's reviewer verdict is a
`ReviewStatus` with Codex's word beside it, and the auto-review row says
"Auto-approved", "Auto-denied" and so on from it; `CommandWork.action` is
gone. `Capabilities` is `{ cloud_relay, kinds }`: the kinds come from the
platform (terminal Claude only with a Unix terminal) rather than a fixed list
of three, and a paired host's fleet entry carries the version and
capabilities its handshake gave while it is reachable. Every top-level enum's
values carry the enum's prefix (`PHASE_STARTING`, `STOP_MODE_GRACEFUL`,
`TRUST_TRUSTED`...), and a test pins the documented zero defaults.

2026-10-09 — **An agent's catalogue is a blob, read with GetBlob; GetCatalogue answers only for a host's providers.**
An agent already hashed the exact bytes of its catalogue, but wrote them to a
`catalogues/` directory of their own, and the daemon decoded them to serve
`GetCatalogue(agent_id)`, re-encoded them to check a peer's copy and wrote the
replica copy re-encoded. A catalogue from a newer agent with a field this
daemon does not know therefore changed hash on the way and was refused. The
agent now writes its catalogue as a blob (`Effect::WriteBlob`, under
`blobs/`) before the step whose snapshot names it, and a client reads it with
`GetBlob(agent_id, snapshot.catalogue)`, decodes it and caches it under the
hash it asked for; a replica keeps the origin's bytes as they came. The
replica blob sweep never evicts the catalogue a replica's current snapshot
names, so a picker keeps its offers while the origin is away; a catalogue no
longer named goes like any blob. `Catalogue.hash` is gone: the hash is the
blob's name. `GetCatalogue` is `{ host_id, provider }` and answers a
`CatalogueBlob { hash, bytes }`, the daemon's copy encoded once and named by
the hash of exactly those bytes, which is what the host's entry names.
`GetBlobResponse` is the bytes alone.

2026-10-09 — **A message's sender is its caller, a paired host is answered only for its host's own agents, and a create carries its kind's settings as bytes.**
`ClientService.SendMessage` took a whole `Envelope`, so a caller could fill in
the sender, the kind (finished, failed) and an incarnation; it now takes a
`SendMessageRequest { id, to, text, context }` and the daemon stamps the
sender from the socket the call came in on: the person, or the agent whose
tools socket made it. Finished and failed messages come only from the
daemon's outbox. `PeerService.SendMessage` keeps the stamped envelope, and the
receiving daemon still takes an agent sender only if that agent belongs to
the calling host. The peer service answers only for this host's own agents:
its inventory stream carries this host's entry and agents, never what this
host knows of others, and `Subscribe`, `Fetch`, `Get` and `SendInput` for an
agent this host only replicates are `NOT_FOUND`, where before they were
answered from the replica or reached its owner's daemon. A client's
`SubscribeRequest` is `{ agent_id, tail }`; the cursor a replica resumes from
lives only on the peer's `PeerSubscribeRequest`. `Dump` answers a client with
`DumpReport { report_path }` and a paired host with its `DumpPart`, instead
of one response carrying both. `CreateAgentRequest` names its host with a
`HostRef` (an id or a name, the shape the front door's `PeerRef` had and now
shares), its settings as `Kind kind` plus the kind's create config encoded in
`bytes config`, read by the spawning host as the kind says and refused when
they do not decode, and passed on untouched by a forwarding daemon; its first
prompt, and a resume's, is a `PromptSubmission`, so a client cannot send
anything but a prompt there and the daemon's "not a prompt" refusal is gone.

2026-10-09 — **A person's input is opaque bytes of its kind; what only the daemon may send moves to the control socket.**
A paired host could call `SendInput` with an `Input.agent_message` naming any
sender, and the agent's interpreter took the envelope as given, bypassing the
rule that a host speaks only for its own agents; a tools socket or a create's
first prompt could carry one too. `Input` is now `{ input_id, kind, body }`,
the body the kind's own input message encoded. Daemons forward it untouched,
so an arm or field a daemon does not know reaches a newer agent intact; the
daemon decodes a copy only for analytics and passes on one it cannot read.
Agent messages, dump requests and a Codex agent's new name are their own
`CtlFrame` arms (`agent_message`, `dump_request`, `rename`), sent only by the
agent's daemon, and the agent's verdict is `Verdict { id }`, keyed by the
input id or the envelope id. The spec seeds the child's queue from a
`Bootstrap` (a prompt, or a parent's message on a parent-driven resume), so a
client's first prompt must be a prompt. Answers are typed inside each kind:
`ClaudeAnswer` and `CodexAnswer` carry the ask key, and Codex's separate
`Approve` became `CodexAnswer.approve`, still refused unless the ask offered
that decision. The remote key vocabulary went: terminal Claude's
permission-mode cycle is the one keystroke a client sends
(`CyclePermissionMode`); the generic key path in the agent and its hard-coded
Up arrow went with it. On an agent's tools socket the one input accepted is an
interrupt to its own child. A stop or a terminal mode this side cannot read
is refused rather than taken as graceful or files. The interpreter fixtures
write agent messages and renames as their own events, and the facts ring
records them as `agent_message` and `rename` entries, redacted in dumps.

2026-10-09 — **The check-in test waits for the check-in to be written down.**
The daemon records its daily check-in and then writes the time to the
profile's `checked_in` file. The test read the file as soon as it saw the
event, and on a Windows runner the write had not landed yet; it now waits
for the file to hold the check-in's time.

2026-10-09 — **Smaller shipped binaries, built for speed, with their symbols kept.**
The `release` profile is now what ships, for the daemon and the phone alike,
and what perf runs measure: fat LTO, one codegen unit and line tables. The
separate `mobile` profile, which optimised the phone's Rust for size, is gone;
the phone's Rust is optimised for speed like the daemon's. The phone had
never actually had LTO: the bridge crate was also built as an rlib, and with
an rlib alongside, rustc keeps each crate's object in the static library and
skips the merge, so the bridge is now a static library only (one merged
object, 9.2 MB of code). The Release app links with `-no_exported_symbols`,
because the linker treated every global Rust symbol the bridge exported as
live and could not dead-strip it (3.2 MB of export table alone). The bundled
SQLite leaves out full-text search, R-trees, JSON, statistics tables and
loadable extensions, none of which the store uses, and the phone's log
filter parses `RUST_LOG` with `Targets` instead of `EnvFilter`, dropping the
regex engine; the journeys' directives parse the same. The phone's binary is
16.9 MB, as before, now speed-optimised (6.98 → 7.95 MB zipped; the same
build with size optimisation would be 13.5 MB, 6.47 MB zipped). The macOS
daemon goes from 28.7 MB (v0.8.0) to 22.1 MB. Releases strip each binary and
publish its symbols beside it (`scripts/release-symbols.sh`: a debuglinked
`.debug` on Linux, a dSYM zip on macOS, the PDB on Windows); a stripped macOS
address symbolicates to file and line through the published dSYM. The
phone's development builds link a new `phone-dev` profile, the release
profile without LTO, because LTO took a core edit's bridge rebuild from 30 s
to 1:39 and the library from 89 MB to 478 MB of embedded bitcode and line
tables. `dev` builds carry no debug information at all: line tables gave
every test and tool binary a dSYM, a third of a tree's `target/`.

2026-10-08 — **The Codex views test no longer races the thread.**
Two attached views of one Codex agent share its thread, so the second view
draws the thread's "user: from the first" whenever that arrives. The test
looked for any "from the first" in the second view and failed on Linux when
the thread's item landed first; it now checks only for the first view's
typed line, which is that view's own.

2026-10-08 — **CI's second run: a stale contract name and three late settlers.**
The contracts check named an interpreter test the protocol-gaps cleanup
deleted with the queue it held (every provider now has a carrier for agent
messages); the name is gone from the contract. Three phone components, the
resume composer, the composer holding a review and the overview's
uncommitted comparison, changed after reporting ready on a CI runner (a
two-point settle of their text), which IOS.md says to mark `settlesLate`;
they are marked.

2026-10-08 — **Terminal journeys lay out alike on macOS and Linux.**
On macOS /tmp is a link to /private/tmp, and a program prints the physical
path, eight cells longer than Linux's. The driver respelled the path text,
but cannot move what was laid out around it: the new agent's composer edge
is right-aligned and its model picker opens under the model field, so that
screen sat eight columns apart on the two platforms. Terminal journeys now
run in one fixed folder whose prefix is the same physical width everywhere
(/private/tmp on macOS, /tmp/journey on Linux), with the test network's
fixed `net` folder inside it, so nothing on screen is random; frames spell
the prefix /tmp/journey, whole or in the pieces a dialog leaves showing.
Journeys in other checkouts wait on a lock, as the phone's do. Every
terminal golden showing a path is re-recorded for the new spelling.

2026-10-08 — **CI's first run of the merged work, fixed where the tests were wrong.**
The terminal's plan frames replay recordings with real timestamps and print
them on the machine's clock, so they read 09:00 where they were recorded and
08:00 on CI; the terminal's own tests now read clocks in UTC (`local_time`),
the fixed rows' time is 14:07 UTC, and the plan goldens read 08:00 in any
zone. A settings test read the model list before the host's catalogue had
arrived, which it may after the first turn; it waits for both. On Windows,
three tests ran what Windows does not host: terminal Claude's catalogue, both
attach tests (terminal Claude, and Codex's own app, macOS and Linux only), and
the live Codex recordings, made over Codex's socket where Windows uses stdio;
they are Unix only. The untracked-paths test wrote names that, under Windows'
temporary folder, passed its 260-character path limit, so git saw no files;
its Windows names are shorter and more numerous.

2026-10-08 — **Main's usage events are merged with the protocol-gaps work.**
Main's usage events met this branch's new answers: an answer's ask is now
also read from a reply in place of answering (a question) and from Codex's
plan answer (a plan), which the event's classifier did not know. The rest
was both sides kept: the daemon carries both its analytics and the worktree
maker, a forwarded send records its usage and settles a never-sent forward
as host unreachable, the phone's shell takes the Share Usage switch, and the
catalogue's home filter string, gone with the filter, stays gone.

2026-10-08 — **A report's picture of the screen masks what moves with the run.**
The phone's `report` journey failed on most runs: its "refused" screen shows
the frozen fleet as a picture, and the agent's age in that picture ("1s" when
recorded, "2s" or more since) is pixels, not an element, so the age's own
volatile mark could not reach it. The journey now remembers the volatile
surfaces on screen when the system photographs the app, and masks them again,
shrunk, wherever `report.frame` draws that photograph. A run with the age at
"7s" against the recorded "1s" passes. Pinning the phone's clock was
rejected: an age compares the host's real start time with the phone's clock,
so it would mean faking time in both, inside the product.

2026-10-08 — **Forms are checked and encoded by the view, typed.**
Each client turned a tool server's form into the answer itself, and the two
disagreed. Defaults: the phone started each field from the view's text
`initial` (the schema's default, else "false" for a toggle and the first
option for a choice), so a required choice was answered before the person
chose anything; the terminal ignored `initial` and started every field
empty, defaults included. Toggles: the phone always sent one; the terminal
left an untouched toggle out, and refused a required one as "is required".
Numbers: the terminal refused text that was not a number at Enter, the phone
held Submit back; both read "inf" and "NaN" as numbers, the terminal then
sending null and the phone dropping the whole content to `{}`; the terminal
sent a whole number for a decimal field as `3.0`. Text: the terminal trimmed
it, the phone sent spaces and let a field of spaces satisfy "required".
Neither checked the limits a schema can set. Now each `FormField` carries
its limits (text length, a number's range, how many picks) and an `initial`
`FormValue` (typed text, a toggle, a choice or picks by position) from the
schema's default only, a toggle off and a choice unchosen. `form_problems`
gives each field's typed `FieldProblem` (required and empty, not a number,
not whole, below or above the range, too short or long, too few or many
picked) and `form_answer` builds the Submit with the JSON object the schema
describes: text trimmed, a whole number sent whole, picks in the options'
order, an untouched toggle off, empty optional fields left out. The phone
reaches the check through a new bridge call, holds Submit back on it and says
a changed field's problem under it; it submits values, not JSON, and Rust
encodes them. The terminal calls both directly and words the problems beside
the field and on the review. Both clients' own encoding is gone. The Swift
generator now writes `null` for a variant holding an optional, which it
wrote as `{}` before; serde refused that, so a new agent's "back to the
default" pick never parsed. Noticeable: the phone's choices start unchosen
(a "Choose" row) unless the server named a default; the terminal starts
fields at their defaults, toggles on No and ticked; the phone's number
keyboard takes a minus sign; problems read "needs a whole number", "needs at
least 1" in the terminal and "Enter a whole number", "At least 1" on the
phone.

2026-10-08 — **Settings, model names and the new-agent pickers come from the view, typed.**
Each client worked out parts of an agent's settings for itself. The running
model's name: the terminal preferred the interpreter's name, the phone
never received it and showed the raw id, so terminal Claude read
"claude-sonnet-5" on the phone and an alias could read differently on each
side. Whether a setting could change: the settings view carried English
sentences, and each client guessed changeability from them and from the
agent's kind. The model chip: the phone showed the effort or else the
current permission, normal or not; the terminal showed the model, effort and
only an unusual permission or mode. And a new agent's pickers: no view built
them, so both clients filtered the host's catalogue themselves, each with
its own copy of which permissions a model takes and its own rule for what a
model change does. The settings view now names every choice (no empty
display name to fall back from; the running model by the interpreter's
name), marks Codex's unnamed settings `custom`, and carries a typed
`Changeable` per setting (a pick, the agent's own cycle, typing its own
named command, or not offered) instead of sentences. `controls(state)`
hands both clients one `ControlsSummary`: the model's name, the effort in
force, and the permission and mode only while they are not the normal ones.
`new_agent_settings` builds a new agent's pickers from a host's catalogue in
the same choice types, and `new_agent_pick` applies a pick: another model
starts at its own default effort and gives up a permission it does not take
for the normal one, picking the normal mode leaves the mode unchosen, and a
chosen value the host does not list stays listed. The phone reaches both
through two new bridge calls; both clients' copies are gone. Noticeable: the
phone names the running model as the terminal does ("Fake 1", "Sonnet 5");
its chip reads "model · effort", then an unusual permission (red when it
acts without asking) and mode, and no longer names the normal permission;
the terminal's Ctrl+S says an effort or model the agent has not offered
rather than opening a one-item list; in a new agent, changing a Claude model
leaves the effort to the model (Claude names no default), a Codex model
starts at its default effort, a permission the model does not take goes
back to the normal one, and a model the host does not offer is listed last;
counts of one read "1 line" (and "1 step" in the terminal) on both clients.

2026-10-07 — **The chat's judgements come from the view, typed.**
Four things in a chat were worked out by each client on its own, from text,
and the two disagreed. A plan's title: the terminal lifted only a `#`
heading and dropped one that just said "plan", the phone lifted any first
line. A refused prompt's reason: both compared the wire's reason strings
and worded what they recognised, and the terminal's exited-agent path had a
notice of its own. An edit's diff: each client parsed the patch, both
treating any line starting `---` or `+++` as a file header, so a removed
`-- comment` or an added `++i` vanished from the preview. And a tool call's
state: whether a call waited on the person was guessed from the row's
attention and decision, differently on each side. The view now hands each
over as a value. A plan ask and plan row carry the title and body split by
the terminal's rule. A refusal is a `RefusalReason`, mapped once from the
wire's reasons, which now live in one place every side refuses from. An
edit ask carries the patch as parsed lines with typed hunk starts, its
counts and the line its first change lands on; header lines are dropped
only outside a hunk, and a file Codex creates or deletes whole reads as
added or removed lines rather than none. Every call row carries a
`CallPhase`, with `Asking` set when an open ask points at the call and
nothing has decided it. Both clients word these and decide nothing; the
terminal's dead row-drawing duplicates went with them. Noticeable: the
phone titles a plan only by its heading; a draining host reads "its host is
shutting down", and closed asks, prompts no longer queued and unreachable
hosts get words of their own on both clients; the terminal's refused send
to an exited agent comes back to the composer with "not sent: it had
exited"; the terminal's "line N" beside an edit is its first change, and
the phone marks where each hunk starts; a created file counts its lines; a
call announced but asking nobody reads "Running" on the phone rather than
"Wants to run"; an asked Codex file change reads "Wants to edit" in the
terminal, and a refused one "Denied" rather than "Edited".

2026-10-07 — **The fleet's judgements come from the view, typed.**
Both clients worked out parts of the fleet themselves, and disagreed. The
terminal counted needing-you by family and the phone by visible row; each
decided that Exited starts folded; both compared the host's exit cause as
text, so a finished one-shot agent read "exited · finished" in a chat and a
stopped one "exited · stopped"; and each decided a host's reach its own way,
the phone checking the host before an agent's ending and ignoring the
row's loud member. The fleet view now hands over each as a value: counts of
agents (not families) that need the person and that are working or
starting, across the whole fleet whatever is folded; whether each section
starts folded; how an agent ended (finished, ended, or failed with the
host's own account) on the card and on the chat's phase; and one reach per
host — online over a route, away for a reason this machine can name (the
relay sees it, this machine is signed out, the host no longer trusts it),
or offline, which a host nobody knows about also is. The family header
counts who needs the person across the whole family, grandchildren and
the parent's side included. Both clients word these and decide nothing.
Noticeable: stopped agents read "exited", finished ones "finished"; the
terminal's hosts window says "away" for a host this machine cannot reach
because it signed out or was distrusted; the phone puts an exited agent's
ending before its host's state, counts starting agents as working, and
drops the needs-you dot on an expanded family's head.

2026-10-07 — **Interpreter checkpoints no longer read older shapes.**
39 fields of the three interpreters' saved state, and of the part they
share, carried a fallback so a checkpoint written before the field existed
still loaded. Nothing older needs reading before the first release, so the
fallbacks are gone and a checkpoint must hold every field. The fallbacks on
the formats amux reads from Claude and Codex, on facts and on authored
fixtures stay, since those legitimately leave fields out. The committed
debug bundle's checkpoint gains the two fields it predated.

2026-10-07 — **Claude's snapshots name the permission `permission`.**
Both Claude snapshots called the setting `permission_mode` while the Codex
snapshot and both create requests call it `permission`; the snapshots now
use `permission` too. Claude's own protocol keeps its name for it.

2026-10-07 — **The terminal folds tool steps by the shared view.**
The terminal asked the view for every row and then decided again itself
which steps of a run show, so the two rules could drift. It now passes its
choice (collapse, show all, hide) and its open runs to the view and draws
only the steps the view shows; what it still decides is the drawing: a
header over an opened run, the newest few steps of one under way, the
folded line, a kept failure. Two differences came out. Under hide, the view
kept a subagent call showing, because its list of tool kinds left subagents
out; every step of a run now hides, as the option says, which the phone
also gets. And the terminal showed every step of a run opened before
switching to hide; hide now hides it.

2026-10-07 — **The protocol is cleaned up as an unreleased one.**
Nothing depends on an older build yet, so the protobuf schemas stop
carrying compatibility they do not need. All 31 `reserved` lines are gone
and every message's fields and every enum's values are renumbered in
reading order. Unused items are deleted: three error details nothing
returns (`BlobMissing`, `BlobTooLarge`, `DiffUnavailable`), six request
messages the profile service never takes, `ProfileInfo`'s `startup_error`
and `minimum_version`, and Codex's `resume_thread_id`. `PROTOCOL_VERSION`
resets to 1. The only-add check (`just proto-check`, its baseline and its CI
step) is removed, since it blocked exactly these changes and steered agents
into reservations; the architecture and wire docs now say version-skew
discipline starts at the first release, and AGENTS.md tells agents to
delete and renumber rather than reserve. The committed debug bundle is
re-encoded field by field from the old numbers to the new ones, so its
content is unchanged. A store, journal or running agent from an earlier
build is not read correctly after this change and must start fresh, and the
deployed relay must run this build before signed-in hosts can link through
it.

2026-10-07 — **What the protocol-gaps work left behind is deleted.**
An audit of everything the work added found the old runtime paths it
replaced already gone, but a layer of dead code the compiler cannot flag
because it is public or only its own tests call it. Deleted: the claude
crate's version cache, transcript wrapper and two launch helpers; three
Codex client settings, a notification queue nothing read and a test-only
re-registration; four pairing, relay and discovery leftovers in the node;
the interpreter's agent-message queue for a provider with no injection
channel; the unused `explores` helpers; spec-driver methods and options no
spec sets; the fake Codex view's pre-socket mode (`--remote` is now
required); three view fields no client reads (a queued prompt's `mine`, the
frame's `mode`, a paired peer's `paired_at_ms`); two whole phone files and
about ten unused phone functions; 66 catalogue strings no source uses; and
`scripts/ios_testnet.py` and an unreferenced architecture image. The
stand-ins check went too: every absence it held is in the deletion ledger,
and what it held present is covered by tests. Stale wording about the
strip, the outbox, stretches and the "Running" section is fixed, and the
phone golden "chat-strip" is now "chat-turn".

2026-10-07 — **A killed test network takes its Bonjour adverts with it.**
Each served host's `dns-sd -P` advertiser outlived a test network that was
SIGKILLed or terminated, and later phone discovery runs saw renamed
duplicates such as "desk (4)". `dns-sd` now runs under a shell tied to its
owner by a pipe and dies when that pipe closes, however the owner ends, and
`testnet serve` shuts down cleanly on SIGTERM.

2026-10-07 — **A refused agent name is a reason, worded by each client.**
The name rule returned an English sentence from Rust. It now returns
`AgentNameProblem` (empty, too long, or characters outside the rule); the
daemon's error, the terminal and the phone each say it in their own words,
so shared code carries meaning and the clients carry the copy.

2026-10-07 — **The phone's local-network story holds its refusal.**
The journey refuses the local network through the debug door, which set
the Hosts store's permission once. The real browser kept reporting its own
state, and the account's profile coming up handed the store the
permission last reported, so either could overwrite the refusal before the
screen was taken, and the story failed whenever they landed after the door.
The door's stand-in now holds for the launch: the real browser stops
reporting and the door waits for the profile before it sets the
permission.

2026-10-07 — **An agent's name is a word a branch can be.**
A worktree's branch is the agent's name as given, so a name git refuses,
such as "fix login", failed the create. Rather than translate names into
branches, a name is now lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, starting
with a letter or digit, at most 64 characters (`wire::agent_name_problem`),
so the same word is the branch, the worktree's folder and the handle on a
command line. The daemon refuses any other name on a create and on a
rename with `INVALID_ARGUMENT`; the spawn tool's schema states the rule; the
terminal's name fields and the phone's rename card say why a typed name
will not do before it is sent, and will not save it.

2026-10-07 — **Home's middle section is "Live".**
It holds starting, working and idle agents, so "Running" over a list of
idle agents, with the phone's subtitle counting "0 running", read wrong.
The shared view's section is now `Live` on both clients, and the phone's
subtitle counts "working", as the terminal's top line does.

2026-10-07 — **A trimmed command's output says so.**
A long Codex command keeps only its newest output, and its row then began
partway through with nothing to say so. The view's command row now carries
`output_trimmed`, set when the interpreter dropped the output's start, and
both clients draw a faint "earlier output trimmed" line above what is left.

2026-10-07 — **A tool server's form is read once, in the shared view.**
The terminal and the phone each parsed the form's JSON schema, the phone
with a tokenizer of its own to keep the schema's order, and they had
drifted: the phone read a field of several picks as text and sent a string
where the server asked for an array. The view's form body now carries the
fields, in the schema's order, each with its kind (text, number, toggle,
one choice or several picks), title, description, whether it is required
and what it starts holding. Both clients draw from those; the phone draws
several picks as a switch per option and answers with an array.

2026-10-07 — **The phone reads a host moving at once.**
Spacing the phone's fleet reads 250 ms apart also delayed the read that
shows a host has come current, so a phone reconnecting through the relay
reached its reconciled fleet about 240 ms later (1244 ms median against a
1007 ms baseline). Each wake now takes its changes first: a host moving is
read at once, and only agents' changes soon after a read wait out the
spacing, with one read taking everything owed. Relay reconciliation is
back to 996 ms and streaming CPU stays at 33%.

2026-10-07 — **The phone reads the fleet at most four times a second.**
Since home wakes when a working agent's step moves, a streaming turn woke
it many times a second, and the phone read and laid out the whole fleet on
the main thread for every wake, even with a chat covering home. The
measured streaming run's main-thread CPU rose from about 34% to 56%, past
its tolerance over the baseline. A fleet wake that comes within 250 ms of
the last read now waits out the rest of that time; the runtime does not
wake again until the changes are taken, so the one later read takes them
all. A wake after a quiet spell still reads at once. Streaming CPU measures
33% again.

2026-10-07 — **The phone's Overview says when nothing has changed.**
After the folder's changes were committed or reverted between turns, the
header still carried the last turn's totals (by design, until the next
turn), and the Overview chose its empty wording from those totals, so a
listing that came back with no files read "Listing the changed files…"
forever. A listing that came back empty now reads "Nothing changed"; the
waiting wording shows only before any listing has answered. The header's
totals still move only at turn ends.

2026-10-07 — **The settings-picks test fetches a catalogue the way a client does.**
The test that sends every settings pick to a copy of each interpreter
handed the chat state a published catalogue before committing the step
whose snapshot names it. Once the chat state started keeping the
catalogue the newest snapshot names over one it does not, Codex's second
start-up catalogue arrived while the first was still the named one and was
dropped, so Codex offered no picks at all. The test now commits the step
first and fetches its catalogue after, as a client does; what it asserts
is unchanged.

2026-10-07 — **Headless Claude's usage-window helpers each say what they do.**
The usage-reset fix slid its new helper under the comment of the one after
it, leaving one stacked comment over three ideas, one of them about window
labels that now live elsewhere. Each helper carries its own comment again
and the stray paragraph is gone; no code changed.

2026-10-07 — **The phone keeps what was typed into a tool server's form.**
A question card's picks and note were kept on the chat and survived leaving
it, but a tool server's form held its values in the card itself, so going
back to the fleet and returning while the form still stood emptied it. The
chat now keeps the form's values by field name on the head ask, the same
way and for as long as a question card's progress: until that ask closes,
so the next form starts as its server wrote it. The tool-server-asks phone
story leaves the chat mid-form, comes back, and photographs the values
still there before submitting them.

2026-10-07 — **A late older catalogue no longer blanks a chat's controls.**
The chat state kept whichever catalogue a fetch returned last, and shows
models, permissions and modes only from the one the newest snapshot names,
so an older catalogue answering after a newer one emptied those controls
until the next session event. Codex publishes two catalogues back to back
at start, so a chat on a new Codex agent could hit it. A held catalogue the
newest snapshot names is now never replaced by one it does not name; the
runtime still caches every fetched catalogue by hash.

2026-10-07 — **A Claude usage window's stated limit ends when it resets.**
Headless Claude states one usage window's status at a time and reports
every window's use, so amux keeps the last status stated for each window.
It never cleared it, so a weekly window once stated near or reached kept
reading that way after it reset, at a few percent used. A report whose
reset for a window is later than the one held now drops the status stated
for it, back to unknown, before the report is applied. A new interpreter
fixture plays a reached weekly window followed by a week-later report that
names only the five-hour window.

2026-10-07 — **Home redraws a working agent's step as it moves.**
A session woke the fleet's home only for what arrived outside its rows, so
when a working agent moved from one tool step to the next with no snapshot
in between, home kept drawing the previous step until something else woke
it; the terminal has no tick on home and the phone reads the same wake. A
session now remembers the line home draws for its agent (the fleet's
`session_line`, read with no age) and wakes home when a row batch changes
it: a new running step, the step ending, what the agent last said. Rows
that leave the line as it was still never wake home. `ui-runtime` now links
`ui-view` for that line.

2026-10-07 — **Claude's messaging socket writes typed lines.**
The auth line and the user message amux writes to terminal Claude's
